messages:
Sam: Quick check — if we let org-scoped service API keys impersonate within projects, how do we avoid elevation when a target project grants broader roles?
Jaya: Are you thinking inheritance (org -> project) or the other way? normally project is narrower, but grants can be wide.
Sam: Right. Example: org-key used by infra svc to call billing in project-A; project-A has a role that also includes admin perms for billing buckets.
Miguel: Two basic models: 1) always evaluate the key's scope first and fail early, 2) evaluate target project's bindings and apply intersection. Both have tradeoffs.
Katie: Intersection seems safer: effective permissions = key_scope ∩ project_bindings. That avoids key getting more perms than intended.
Jaya: Intersection is safe but breaks a lot of current flows where admins expect org-keys to be accepted as full delegates. Backcompat risk.
Miguel: Also complexity: we need to materialize effective roles at request-time. That implies extra lookup latency and caching.
Sam: What about explicit deny rules? Could we allow deny at project boundary to override intersection?
Katie: Deny semantics are sharp but add surprises. If a project admin adds a deny, org tooling could break silently. We need visibility/audit.
Jaya: Proposal: default = intersection (least privilege). Add a opt-in "delegation: broad" flag on org-keys that preserves org-level perms when accepted by projects. Require project whitelisting to accept broad delegation.
Sam: I like whitelisting. Add audit requirement: project must explicitly opt-in with a signed acceptance manifest.
Miguel: Implementation sketch: at auth-time fetch key_policy (cached), fetch project_acceptance (cached, TTL 1m), compute effective roles. If key has delegation:broad and project_acceptance=true then effective_roles = key_roles ∪ project_roles else effective_roles = key_roles ∩ project_roles.
Katie: Need to handle deny precedence: always apply explicit denies from the project after union/intersection to avoid accidental escalations.
Jaya: Also mention impersonation chains — if svcA impersonates svcB, we need to propagate original principal and ensure each hop enforces its own intersection/whitelist. Chain eval could be expensive.
Sam: Performance concerns: can we use a precomputed matrix for common projects + keys to avoid per-request DB hits? Maybe warm caches from RBAC service as soon as keys are issued/updated.
Miguel: Yes, proactively push key->project accepted bindings into the serving layer on change events. Fallback to remote eval if cache miss.
Katie: UX: surface "why denied" in logs with the delta (key_roles vs project_roles vs denies). That will help troubleshoot when intersection blocks a flow.
Jaya: Migration story: default to intersection, run a 30-day opt-in window where projects can whitelist existing org-keys. Emit policy-compat reports to owners.
Sam: Good. One more edge: API routing — we sometimes route by key prefix to different frontends. If a key is both org and project scoped (legacy), ensure routing keeps correct tenant header so project acceptance check hits right project.
Miguel: Noted. Add unit tests: chain length 3 impersonations, denied role at middle hop, cache expiry scenarios.
Katie: I'll draft a short RFC with the opt-in whitelist + audit + caching plan and the compatibility timeline.
Sam: Thanks — tagging @Jaya and @Miguel for design review. :thumbsup:
